record.original_question: Does there exist an integer k such that if two positive integers m and n satisfy R(m + i) = R(n + i) for every i = 0, ..., k - 1, then m = n?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.2 (Erdős-Woods). There exists a positive integer k such that, for m and n positive integers, the conditions R(m + i) = R(n + i) (i = 0, . . . , k − 1) imply m = n.

artifact.self_contained_problem: For a positive integer n, let R(n) denote the radical of n, that is, the product of the distinct prime divisors of n (with R(1) = 1); equivalently, R(n) = R(m) if and only if n and m have the same set of prime divisors. Decide whether there exists a positive integer k with the following property: for all positive integers m and n, if R(m + i) = R(n + i) for every i ∈ {0, 1, …, k − 1}, then m = n.
artifact.status_search_result: The Erdős–Woods conjecture in this radical-based formulation is generally reported as still open. Related work (Dowe 1989; Cégielski–Heroult–Richard 2003) studies Erdős–Woods numbers (a related but distinct notion derived from a stronger statement of Woods that was refuted), proving for instance that there are infinitely many such numbers and that the set is recursive, but the existence of a uniform k as in the conjecture has not been established or refuted.

status_evidence.title: Erdős–Woods number — Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Dowe (1989) proved that there are infinitely many Erdős–Woods numbers; Cégielski, Heroult & Richard (2003) showed the set is recursive.
status_evidence.claim: Research on Erdős–Woods numbers continues; the central conjecture about uniform k for radical-determined integers remains a standing open problem.

status_evidence.title: On Erdős–Wood's conjecture, Proc. Math. Sci.
status_evidence.snippet: Article addressing partial results toward the Erdős–Woods conjecture.
status_evidence.claim: Partial results exist but the conjecture is not resolved.
